Paragraph1: "Oregon’s pioneering decriminalization effort for drugs will end on Sunday, when a new statute takes effect and once again makes possession of small quantities of hard drugs a crime. Under HB4002, anyone found with substances such as fentanyl, heroin or meth can either face a possession charge or opt for treatment that includes a behavioral‑health program and a deflection initiative designed to avoid fines. Simple possession is classified as a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months in jail. The law intends to give police more leeway to crack down on drug use in public spaces and to impose tougher penalties on those who sell drugs near parks."

Paragraph2: "While the statute encourages counties to develop treatment alternatives that steer people away from the criminal justice system and toward addiction and mental‑health services, it does not mandate such programs. Supporters argue this flexibility lets each county shape services according to its available resources, whereas critics warn it may produce a confusing and uneven patchwork of rules across the state."

Paragraph3: "Portland police chief Bob Day explained that eligibility for deflection is tightly limited: a person must have no other charges, no outstanding warrants, no violent behavior and be medically stable. When someone meets these conditions, officers call the county’s deflection dispatch line, provide basic information, verify eligibility and connect the individual to a mobile behavioral‑health outreach team that has thirty minutes to make contact. If the team cannot arrive within that window, the person is taken to jail; officers said they cannot simply wait longer."

Paragraph4: "The changes will affect residents of every age across the country, influencing everyday choices such as where to eat, what to shop for, and even how they use their tongue in conversation, highlighting the broad reach of the new policy."
